reviews.evidence: This is a navigation section listing group concepts and defines no mathematical object, so its empty prerequisite list is correct.
The proposition assumes an abelian group and subgroup and concludes normality; the three targets define exactly commutativity, subgroup closure, and conjugation invariance.

The definition is the kernel of the sign map on S_n. Reading the target definitions confirms finite-permutation supplies S_n and permutation-sign supplies inversion-parity sign; kernel, group, and subgroup supply the construction and subgroup scope.
The finite cyclic hypothesis and generator-image map yield Aut(G)≅(Z/nZ)^×; cyclic-subgroup, group-isomorphism, and group-of-units supply the displayed objects.
The finite action theorem averages cardinalities of Fix(g) to count orbits; group, action, fixed-point-set, and orbit are each explicit terms.
The theorem assumes finite G with |G|=p^a q^b and concludes solvability; group and solvable-group are the direct hypothesis/output concepts.
The proposition derives left/right cancellation by multiplying by inverses in a group; group is the sole defining input.
For finite G and p∣|G| the conclusion supplies an element and cyclic subgroup of order p; group and cyclic-subgroup match the statement.
The left translations define an injective group homomorphism G→Sym(G); group, homomorphism, monomorphism, and left-multiplication-action support each construction.
The proposition takes Z(G) and proves every automorphism preserves it; group, center, and characteristic-subgroup are direct terms.
The core defines Z(G) as the subgroup commuting with every x; group and subgroup are defining inputs, while examples and consequences are optional.
The short extension is central when iota(A) lies in Z(E); group-extension and center are direct, and abelian A is an explicitly stated consequence.
C_G(S) is defined as the subgroup of G commuting with every s∈S; group and subgroup directly support the construction.

The definition quantifies automorphisms preserving a subgroup and states characteristic implies normal via inner automorphisms; all five listed concepts occur in definition/equivalent characterization.
A chief series is a finite normal chain with no intermediate normal subgroup; the equivalent quotient-factor formulation requires group, normal-subgroup, and quotient-group.
The finite class equation combines conjugation orbits, centralizers, centers, and orbit-stabilizer class sizes; every listed target supplies a displayed term or derivation.
The proposition partitions a finite group into conjugacy classes, identifies singleton classes with the center, and derives class sizes and the class equation; all listed targets are used.
A class function is a function invariant under xgx⁻¹ and hence constant on conjugacy classes; group, function, and conjugacy-class are direct inputs.
The theorem decomposes a finite abelian group into direct products of cyclic prime-power groups; abelian, direct-product, cyclic, and p-group supply the displayed structures.
The definition is a monoid with ab=ba; monoid is the only defining prerequisite, with zero/ring examples optional.
The core fixes [g,h]=g⁻¹h⁻¹gh for a group; group supplies multiplication and inverses, while center and commutator-subgroup are later remarks.
[G,G] is the subgroup generated by all commutators; group, generated-subgroup, and commutator are exactly the displayed ingredients.
The finite chain is subnormal with simple quotient factors; group, subnormal-series, quotient-group, and simple-group match each defining condition.
Cl_G(g)={xgx⁻¹:x∈G} is defined from a group; conjugacy-class’s later equivalence and partition remarks do not add prerequisites.

The finite-group class-size formula is orbit-stabilizer for the conjugation action: the class is the orbit and C_G(g) the stabilizer, whose index is computed. Conjugation-action is required with group, class, centralizer, index, and orbit-stabilizer.
Conjugacy is defined by h=xgx⁻¹ and c_x is identified as an inner automorphism; group and inner-automorphism directly support the formula.
The formula g·x=gxg⁻¹ is declared a group action; group and group-action supply the ambient operation and axioms.
The proposition verifies self-conjugation as a group action and names the conjugation action; group, group-action, and conjugation-action are explicit.
For y=gxg⁻¹, yⁿ=gxⁿg⁻¹, so group powers and the conjugate-element hypothesis establish equal finite/infinite order.
The assignments A↦A/N and B↦π⁻¹(B) operate between subgroups of G and G/N. Quotient-group is a direct prerequisite alongside group, normal-subgroup, subgroup, and preimage.
Left/right cosets are translates of a subgroup in a group; subgroup and group directly define gH and Hg, while partition/index/quotient are consequences.
The proposition proves every element lies in gH and cosets are equal or disjoint, exactly the partition definition; group, subgroup, coset, and partition are direct.
⟨g⟩={gⁿ:n∈Z} is the smallest subgroup containing g; group, subgroup, and generated-subgroup support the definition.
The index organizes direct/semi-direct products and extensions and defines no standalone object, so no prerequisites are needed.

The recursion uses commutator subgroups, while the core explicitly asserts each term is normal and each factor G^(n)/G^(n+1) is abelian. Group, commutator-subgroup, normal-subgroup, and quotient-group are all required.
G×H with componentwise multiplication uses group factors and the Cartesian product carrier; those are the two direct prerequisites.
The direct sum is the finite-support subgroup of a family’s direct product; group and direct-product-groups supply the family and ambient construction.
The theorem’s actual hypotheses and conclusion concern integers, gcd, φ(n), and modular congruence. Group-of-units and Lagrange are only the proof route in Remarks and are not prerequisites.

The short exact sequence explicitly encodes injective and surjective maps, image/kernel equality, normal kernel, quotient identification, and isomorphisms. Group-isomorphism is required for the stated identifications.
Faithfulness is defined by the action kernel being trivial; group-action, kernel-of-action, and trivial-subgroup directly supply the definition.
Both displayed forms are arithmetic statements for an integer modulo a prime. The unit-group/Lagrange derivation is in Remarks and is not a defining input, so only integers remains.
The proposition assumes a finite cyclic group and constructs φ(k̄)=g^k as an isomorphism. Group, cyclic-subgroup, and group-isomorphism match the hypothesis, powers, and conclusion.
The core concludes with a unique group isomorphism G/ker(f)→im(f), making group-isomorphism an explicit output concept in addition to homomorphism, quotient, kernel, and image.
The theorem identifies the kernel as normal and induces an isomorphism from the quotient to the image. All six listed targets occur in the displayed statement and its surjective specialization.

The core defines X^G for a given group action as points fixed by every group element. Group-action is the sole defining prerequisite; stabilizer and center appear only in equivalent/examples sections.
The finite group G, normal subgroup N, Sylow p-subgroup P of N, and normalizer N_G(P) are explicit hypotheses and terms of G=NN_G(P). The four listed targets directly define them.
Freeness is defined by every stabilizer G_x being trivial. Group-action and stabilizer supply the action and fixed-point subgroup; regular-action is a later consequence only.
The universal property explicitly quantifies a set, functions i and f, groups, and a unique homomorphism. Function was added to the existing set, group, and homomorphism prerequisites.

The theorem assumes a finitely generated abelian group and displays a direct-sum decomposition. Abelian-group and direct-sum-groups supply exactly the hypothesis and construction; PID material is a remark.
The core defines ⟨S⟩ as an intersection of subgroups containing a subset S. Group, subset, intersection, and subgroup are all required for that displayed definition.
The core defines S generating G by ⟨S⟩=G. Group, subgroup, and generated-subgroup provide the ambient object, containment notion, and displayed construction.
An epimorphism is a group homomorphism that is surjective as a function. Those two listed targets state the complete definition; image/quotient occur in optional material.
The definition is a short exact sequence and explicitly identifies N as normal and Q canonically isomorphic to E/N. Group-isomorphism was added for that stated quotient identification.
A monomorphism is defined as a group homomorphism that is injective. The two listed targets exactly supply the definition; kernel/image are later equivalent-characterization consequences.
The displayed presentation is F(S) modulo the normal closure of R and requires S as a set. Free-group, normal-closure, quotient-group, and set directly support each construction.
The definition assumes a finite group and subgroup and sets gcd(|H|,[G:H])=1. Group, subgroup, index, and gcd are direct; Sylow/solvable material is explanatory context retained as linked content.
The image φ(G) is a subset and subgroup of H for a group homomorphism; homomorphism, subgroup, and image supply the definition and conclusion.
The proposition concludes im(f) is a subgroup for a homomorphism; homomorphism, image-group, and subgroup are exactly the hypothesis, object, and output.
A subgroup of index two has equal left/right cosets and is normal; group, subgroup, index, and normal-subgroup match the complete proposition.
Index is the cardinality of left cosets; subgroup, group, cardinality, and coset directly define it, while Lagrange/index-two facts are consequences.

The core defines c_g(x)=gxg⁻¹ as an automorphism and Inn(G) as a subgroup of Aut(G). Group, automorphism-group, and subgroup supply the exact ambient and containment notions; quotient/center facts are later remarks.

The definition requires N,H subgroups, both normal, trivial intersection, and NH=G, then concludes the multiplication map is an isomorphism to a direct product. Intersection-of-subgroups was added for the explicit N∩H condition.
The definition requires N normal, N∩H={e}, NH=G, and uses conjugation H→Aut(N) to identify G with N⋊H. Intersection-of-subgroups was added for the explicit intersection condition.

The proposition defines the intersection of a family of subgroups and proves it is a subgroup, including the empty-intersection=G edge case. Group, subgroup, and set support the quantified family and construction.

The theorem assumes a group with a finite composition series and concludes equal lengths and isomorphic factor multisets. Composition-series, simple-group, and group-isomorphism supply the hypotheses and conclusion.

The core compares two composition series, explicitly quantifies quotient factors and an isomorphism permutation. Group-isomorphism was added for the displayed factor equivalences; quotient and simple-group support each factor.
The kernel is defined as the subgroup φ⁻¹({e_H}) of a homomorphism. Group-homomorphism and subgroup directly support the map and claimed subgroup; normality and quotient are remarks.
The proposition takes a homomorphism and its kernel and concludes normality. The three listed targets exactly supply map, kernel, and conjugation-invariant subgroup conclusion.
The core defines the action kernel as elements fixing every x. Group-action is the direct prerequisite; normality, permutation homomorphism, and faithfulness are consequences stated afterward.

The core proves a homomorphism kernel is normal. Homomorphism, kernel, and normal-subgroup are the only direct terms; quotient and first-isomorphism links are explanatory consequences. Integration classification: the reviewed current source includes a repair relative to the preceding validated commit.

The theorem assumes chain conditions on normal subgroups and compares direct-product decompositions into directly indecomposable factors, concluding isomorphism after permutation. Group, normal-subgroup, direct-product, and group-isomorphism match the statement.
The finite-group theorem partitions G into equal-cardinality cosets and states |G|=[G:H]|H|. Group, subgroup, coset, cardinality, partition, and index each occur in the displayed conclusion.

The definition combines an abelian group, partial order, lattice joins/meets, and translation invariance. The three listed targets provide precisely these structures; homomorphisms are a later morphism section.
The proposition defines g·x=gx and explicitly concludes the action is transitive and free, hence regular. Group, group-action, and regular-action are therefore all justified by the theorem statement.
A loop is defined as a quasigroup with an identity; the unique left/right division conditions are inherited from quasigroup and identity is stated locally. Quasigroup is the direct prerequisite.
The recursion defines γₙ₊₁=[γₙ,G] using the subgroup generated by explicit commutators. Group, commutator, and generated-subgroup supply the displayed construction; nilpotence examples are optional.
The core is exactly a set with a binary operation and no further axioms. Set and binary-operation directly provide both defining ingredients.
The theorem assumes a free group and subgroup, then gives freeness and, under finite rank/index, the formula rank(H)=1+[F:H](n−1). Free-group, subgroup, and index support the hypotheses and equation.

Nilpotence is defined by termination of the lower central series at {e}; group and lower-central-series are the direct defining prerequisites. p-group, quaternion, upper-central, and solvability statements are examples/equivalences.

The core takes a subset A and defines the intersection of all normal subgroups containing it, equivalently the subgroup generated by conjugates. Subset and intersection-of-subgroups were added alongside group, normal-subgroup, and generated-subgroup.
The core defines H◁G by gHg⁻¹=H for every g, with G and H≤G as hypotheses. Group and subgroup are the direct defining inputs; coset, quotient, and conjugation references are explanatory consequences.
The criterion assumes G and N≤G and concludes normality exactly when gng⁻¹∈N. Group, subgroup, and normal-subgroup provide the stated hypotheses and output.
The core defines N_G(H)={g:gHg⁻¹=H} and proves it is a subgroup containing H. Group and subgroup supply the ambient operation and H; normality appears only as an equivalent interpretation.
Given a group action, the core defines G·x={g·x:g∈G}⊂X. Group-action is the direct prerequisite; partition and stabilizer are later consequences.
The lemma assumes a group acting on a set and concludes its distinct orbits partition X. Group, set, orbit, and partition correspond exactly to the hypotheses and output.
The core bijection G/Stab(x)→Orb(x) and finite formulas explicitly use orbit, stabilizer, coset and index notation; the added coset/index edges are required by the displayed statement.

For finite G, the theorem defines ord(g) as least n with gⁿ=e and concludes ord(g)| |G|. The only defining ambient input is a finite group; cyclic-subgroup and Lagrange are explanatory equivalent/corollary links.

The definition combines an abelian group with a translation-invariant total order. Abelian-group and total-order directly provide both structures; positive-cone details are equivalent characterization prose.
Out(G)=Aut(G)/Inn(G) is formed from a normal subgroup Inn(G) of Aut(G); normal-subgroup is required for the quotient construction and was added.
A p-group is defined by element orders p^k, equivalently finite cardinality p^n. Group and cardinality supply the two formulations; center and Sylow links are later remarks.
The theorem assumes a finite p-group of order p^n with n≥1 and concludes its center has size divisible by p. P-group and center are the exact hypothesis/output concepts.
The corollary states p|Z(G)| for a finite p-group and illustrates D₈. P-group and center directly supply the hypothesis and conclusion; the class-equation proof is a remark.
The proposition assumes a finite p-group |G|=p^n and concludes a subgroup of every order p^k, including k=0,n. P-group and subgroup match the structural hypothesis and output.
The proof concludes G is abelian after splitting on |Z(G)| and using G/Z(G) cyclic; abelian-group is an explicit theorem output and was added.
The definition is [G,G]=G, with commutator-subgroup supplying the derived subgroup and group the ambient object. Abelian/simple consequences are examples/equivalences.
The definition is a homomorphism G→Sym(X), equivalently an action, with Sym(X) consisting of bijections. Group, group-homomorphism, bijective-function, and group-action are all direct ingredients.

The theorem defines determinant modulo nth powers on PGL and identifies kernel PSL in a short exact sequence. Projective groups, determinant, and exact-sequence targets support each displayed term and the field-specific examples.
A finite group of prime order has every nonidentity element generate G. Group is the direct hypothesis; Lagrange and cyclic-subgroup occur only in context/conclusion notation.
The proposition assumes two normal subgroups and proves NM=MN and normality using conjugation. Group and normal-subgroup are the exact inputs to the displayed set and proof.
PGL(V)=GL(V)/(k×I) requires a nonzero finite-dimensional vector space, the general linear group, and quotient group. The projective-space action and PSL comparison are later sections.

PSL_n(k) is defined as SL_n(k) modulo its scalar center; the special-linear, quotient, normal-subgroup, and matrix targets support the formula. The projective realization and field caveat are checked in the full source.
The core defines H<G as a subgroup that is a proper subset. Group, subgroup, and proper-subset are exactly the defining inputs.
The core requires unique solutions to ax=b and ya=b, while magma supplies the underlying set and binary operation. The division examples do not impose group axioms.

The page gives Q8’s eight elements and multiplication relations i²=j²=k²=ijk=−1, then checks closure/associativity and noncommutativity. Group is the structural target; division-ring realization is optional.
The quotient is the set of cosets of a normal subgroup with multiplication (gN)(hN)=(gh)N. Normal-subgroup, group, and coset are direct construction inputs.
The factorization f=bar f∘π through G/N and uniqueness use group, normal-subgroup, quotient-group, and homomorphism exactly as listed.
Regularity is defined as free plus transitive, and the equivalent unique transporter property follows. The three listed action targets are direct prerequisites.

The theorem compares finite subnormal series and concludes refinements with isomorphic quotient factors. Group, subnormal-series, quotient-group, and group-isomorphism support the hypotheses and output.
The explicit generator t u (overline{tu})⁻¹ depends on a group, subgroup H, and a transversal; those are the direct structural inputs, with generating details stated locally.

The finite theorem assumes a normal Hall subgroup and concludes existence and conjugacy of complements, equivalently a semidirect product. Group, normal-subgroup, Hall, semidirect-product, and conjugation-action match each assertion.
The map H→HK/K has kernel H∩K and induces H/(H∩K)≅HK/K. Group, subgroup, normal-subgroup, homomorphism, and quotient-group are all displayed inputs/outputs.
The multiplication (n1,h1)(n2,h2)=(n1 φ(h1)(n2),h1h2) requires groups, a homomorphism H→Aut(N), and the automorphism-group target.
A section of an exact sequence induces conjugation Q→Aut(N) and identifies G with N⋊Q. Exact-sequence, split-extension, and semidirect-product are direct hypotheses/conclusion concepts.
Simplicity is defined by a nontrivial group whose only normal subgroups are {e} and G. Group, normal-subgroup, and trivial-subgroup supply all defining terms.
Solvability is termination of the derived series at {e}; group, derived-series, trivial-subgroup, and commutator-subgroup support the recursion and endpoint.
A split extension is an extension with a homomorphic section s and πs=id. Group-homomorphism is the direct prerequisite; semidirect equivalence is later context.
The stabilizer G_x={g:g·x=x} is proved a subgroup for a group action. Group-action and subgroup directly support definition and conclusion.
The core axiomatizes H⊂G by identity, product closure, and inverse closure. Group and subset are the defining ambient and carrier concepts.
The theorem assumes a nonempty subset H of a group and gives xy⁻¹ closure iff subgroup. Group, subset, and subgroup are the hypothesis, test, and conclusion.
The theorem assumes a nonempty subset and tests product and inverse closure for being a subgroup. Group, subset, and subgroup match the complete statement.
The proposition derives identity, inverse, product, and xy⁻¹ closure from H being a subgroup of G. Subgroup and group are the only direct inputs.
The theorem assumes a cyclic group and subgroup and gives explicit generators in finite and infinite cases. Group, cyclic-subgroup, and subgroup support both cases.
A subnormal series is a finite chain with each predecessor normal in its successor. Group and normal-subgroup are the defining prerequisites.
The finite group theorem defines n_p for Sylow p-subgroups and proves n_p≡1 mod p under |G|=p^a m. Group and Sylow-subgroup supply the objects counted.
The lemma places any finite p-subgroup Q inside a conjugate of a Sylow P. Group, Sylow-subgroup, and p-group support the hypotheses and containment conclusion.
If the number of Sylow p-subgroups is one, conjugation fixes P, yielding normality. Group, Sylow-subgroup, and normal-subgroup match the full proposition.
A Sylow p-subgroup is a subgroup of order equal to the largest p-power dividing |G|. Group, subgroup, and p-group support the definition and stated examples.
For |G|=p^a m, the theorem concludes a subgroup of order p^a and names it Sylow. Group, subgroup, and Sylow-subgroup match hypothesis, output, and terminology.
The theorem places each p-subgroup Q inside a conjugate of P and concludes Sylow conjugacy under the conjugation action. Group, Sylow-subgroup, p-group, and conjugation-action support those terms.
The theorem states n_p divides m and n_p≡1 mod p for finite G. Group and Sylow-subgroup supply the counted finite objects; proof links are remarks.
For N⊂K normal in G, the theorem constructs K/N◁G/N and (G/N)/(K/N)≅G/K. Group, normal-subgroup, and quotient-group are direct hypothesis and outputs.
The definition quantifies powers g^n=e and concludes g=e, so group is the only prerequisite. Free groups appear as an example of torsion-free groups, not a defining input.
Transitivity is defined by existence of g sending every x to every y, equivalently one orbit. Group-action is the direct prerequisite.
The trivial subgroup is {e} inside a group. Group and subgroup directly support the identity and subgroup claims.
The proposition proves two identity elements for the same group operation coincide. Group supplies the axioms; binary operation is already part of its definition.
The proposition proves two two-sided inverses of g coincide using group axioms. Group is the sole direct prerequisite.
A unital magma is a magma with a two-sided identity, without associativity. Magma supplies exactly the carrier and operation.
The series starts with {e}, Z(G), and recursively takes preimages of quotient centers. Group, center, and quotient-group are direct construction inputs.
